papers.title: Multicore Quantum Architecture for Scalable and Energy-Aware Green IoT Computing
papers.abstract: The rapid growth of the Internet of Things (IoT) is increasing the computational demand placed on edge and backend processing infrastructures, motivating scalable architectures that can reduce execution and communication overhead. This paper presents a communication-aware comparison of homogeneous multicore classical and quantum architectures for Green IoT using the Qcomm simulator. In addition, a mesh-based, homogeneous, quantum-classical multicore architecture is proposed to enable scalable, efficient execution of distributed quantum workloads. We evaluate a 4x4 mesh of 16 processing cores under regular, classical-bottleneck, and quantum-bottleneck conditions, and study the effects of traffic pattern and Light-to-Matter (LTM) port provisioning on performance. Results show that butterfly traffic yields the largest gains over uniform traffic in both execution time and qubit coherence, while performance benefits from additional LTM ports saturate beyond four ports. At the algorithm level, homogeneous Multi Quantum Processing Units (QPUs) achieve 10x, 9x, and 7x energy efficiency improvements in comparison to Multi-CPUs for Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA), Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE), and Quantum Neural Network (QNN), respectively. The paper's findings show that communication-aware multicore quantum architectures are promising for latency-sensitive IoT processing. Furthermore, the results validate the proposed architecture and provide a foundation for future scheduling and resource management techniques to improve scalability and efficiency in multi-QPU systems.

papers.title: Threat Landscape of Vibe Coding and the Road to Secure Autonomy
papers.abstract: Vibe coding is reshaping software development, enabling faster implementation and allowing individuals with limited programming experience to describe requirements in natural language while AI agents write, test, and deploy the code. As these agents evolve into autonomous systems that execute commands, manage dependencies, access cloud resources, and interact with other agents, their security risks extend beyond incorrect code to actions with direct consequences for software systems. Although research on these risks is expanding, it remains fragmented across areas including prompt injection, insecure code generation, supply-chain attacks, and human factors, with limited consensus on terminology, threat assumptions, and evaluation. This paper consolidates emerging research through the lens of the vibe coding workflow. We establish a reference architecture, characterise six levels of agent autonomy, and develop a threat model centred on five trust boundaries spanning developers, AI models, tools, cloud infrastructure, and the wider software ecosystem. Building on this foundation, we propose a taxonomy of twenty-one threats across nine classes. For each threat, we review the available evidence, assess proposed defences, and identify limitations. Our analysis highlights that risks increase with agents' operational authority, while most defences rely on model judgement and address isolated threats. Finally, we identify eleven research challenges, including enforceable limits on agent authority and shared benchmarks and methodologies for assessing vibe coding security.

papers.title: SLED: Sensor SLicing from Edge to Datacenter
papers.abstract: Modern sensing systems generate large volumes of heterogeneous data streams from multiple sensor modalities, increasing reliance on datacenters for computation, artificial intelligence/superintelligence (AI/SI) inference, and AI/SI training. Each sensor stream may have different network and compute requirements depending on its type and data volume. However, current wireless systems typically allocate resources at the device level, leading to contention among co-located sensor streams, where bulk data transfers may starve latency-critical telemetry. To this end, this paper introduces Sensor Slicing (SL). SL provides deterministic, medium access control (MAC)-level isolation for individual sensors within a single user equipment (UE) in open radio access networks (O-RAN). Using agentic coding techniques, SL is implemented in two O-RAN-compliant packages, reducing development time by 400 times (2 h 40 min [OCUDU] vs. 6.5 weeks [OAI]), 228-fold fewer human prompts (4 vs. 913), and less than half the tokens (0.64B vs. 1.43B). An associated end-to-end framework, SLED, is implemented to establish per-sensor radio and network isolation across edge, campus, and remote high-performance computing (HPC) tiers. Over-the-air wireless experiments demonstrate that while conventional network slicing causes critical delays to increase more than 2,300-fold under high traffic load, SLED maintains stable latency. Scaling evaluations on the two RAN stacks show that throughput remains within 0.9% and 1.4% of expected allocations even as the number of sensor slices increases. The results demonstrate that SLED preserves latency-critical telemetry while effectively utilizing resources across the sensor-to-HPC pipeline. The SLED software and evaluation datasets are publicly available at https://github.com/UNL-CPN-Lab/SLED-Sensor-SLicing-from-Edge-to-Datacenter.

papers.title: Residual-Guided Lightweight Reinforcement Learning for Risk-Aware Trajectory Selection with a Frozen World Model
papers.abstract: In automated driving, world models provide future scene predictions for evaluating candidate trajectories, but fixed selection rules may not capture scene-dependent trade-offs. We propose a residual-guided reinforcement learning (RL) framework for lightweight trajectory selection with a frozen world model and a fixed candidate bank. The framework uses proximal policy optimization (PPO) to fine-tune a joint policy over candidate selection and bounded trajectory residuals. A context-conditioned ranking network learns candidate preferences from feedback obtained by evaluating local perturbations of the selected trajectories. At inference, the selector combines learned preference and predicted risk ranks using fixed weights and returns the selected candidate trajectory without modification. Fine-tuning updates 16,106 parameters across the actor and critic, while the deployed selector retains only the 11,725-parameter ranking network, with the residual branch and critic used exclusively during training. In open-loop evaluation on the nuScenes validation set, the method reduces average Euclidean trajectory error (L2) by 3.99% relative to the RiskWorld model baseline without RL-based selection. Under matched budgets for feedback accesses and actor updates, residual exploration reduces L2 by 0.83% relative to the categorical PPO variant trained without residuals. The method also maintains lower L2 than RiskWorld when risk features are removed or shuffled.

papers.title: MASQ: Measurement-Adaptive Sampling for Near-Clifford Quantum Error Correction Circuits
papers.abstract: Classical sampling of quantum error correction (QEC) circuits supports fault-tolerant protocol evaluation, but estimating rare logical failures requires many independent shots. Frame-active-state simulators isolate non-stabilizer information in a dense active-state vector, yet dense-state processing remains exponential in the active width. This paper presents MASQ, an exact measurement-adaptive sampler for near-Clifford QEC circuits based on selective materialization of non-Clifford rotations. At each measurement boundary, MASQ materializes only rotations in a measurement-relevant closure capturing direct and indirect non-commuting dependencies, deferring the rest to limit active-state expansion. Stabilizer-assisted elimination further removes rotations certified to be invisible to all future measurements. A circuit-dependent schedule is computed once and shared across shots, while adaptive caching of conditional Born probabilities and batched execution reduce repeated sampling work while preserving the measurement-record distribution. Across 19 QEC benchmarks, MASQ reduces peak active width by up to 40 active virtual qubits and achieves up to 8,098-fold CPU throughput speedup over Clifft on multi-round circuits.

papers.title: Automated-Truck Penetration Shapes Human Drivers' Car-Following Margins Near Motorway Ramps: A Driving-Simulator Study
papers.abstract: Automated-vehicle dedicated lanes (AVDLs) are proposed as transitional infrastructure for mixed traffic, but their effect near ramps, and that of automated trucks, on the human drivers sharing the road has rarely been observed. In a mixed-design driving-simulator experiment, 63 drivers were assigned to one of four layouts (an AVDL extending beyond, coinciding with, or ending inside a 1.5-km ramp weaving section, or no AVDL) and drove at four automated-truck penetration levels from 20% to 80%. Linear mixed-effects models with participant random effects and multiplicity control were used. Higher penetration reduced the share of car-following time at gaps below 1.5 s from 28.5% to 18.1% (Holm-adjusted p = .006). This was explained by leader composition: drivers spent 8% of following time behind a truck at 20% penetration and 48% at 80%, kept longer gaps behind trucks, and did not change their gaps within leader type. AVDL layout had no detectable effect on safety margins, rear-end conflict rates, travel time or speed (differences bounded within plus or minus 5 s per section) and no significant effect on workload. Between-driver differences accounted for 52% to 77% of the variance in the main outcomes. Mixed-traffic models should therefore represent human car-following as leader-type-dependent and heterogeneous.

papers.title: A Copper-Inducible Yeast Biosensor with Bioluminescent Readout: Mathematical Modeling, Experimental Validation, and Photodetector Coupling for Molecular Communication in IoBNT
papers.abstract: Engineered living biosensors constitute promising model organisms for bringing Molecular Communications (MC) closer to practical applications. However, challenges associated with their development and characterization have resulted in the relevant literature being limited in the MC domain, . In this paper, we contribute in this direction by leveraging engineered yeast as a basis to detect heavy metals such as copper. The biosensor's development is supported by a validated mathematical characterization and analysis for possible integration in an MC system. Different from the existing literature, mathematical representations of the major biological processes within the yeast copper detoxification pathway are integrated into a comprehensive framework that predicts the time evolution of the CUP1 gene, which is treated as the system output. In the engineered circuit, CUP1 was replaced with GFP, therefore making GFP fluorescence the final system output. Experimental analysis including mRNA transcript quantification and fluorometric measurements, validate the GFP reporting model to a satisfactory degree. This establishes the proposed model as a useful tool for virtual experimentation and the developed testbed as a suitable platform for further engineering of yeast-based copper sensors. The theoretical analysis is further extended by incorporating a self-sustained bioluminescent reporter for yeast, replacing GFP and enabling optical output without external light excitation. The optical response is coupled to a photodetector model, rendering the system suitable for integration into mobile monitoring devices such as Smart Pills. The presented characterization of the yeast receiver as a copper biosensor, constitutes the first step towards the development and characterization of a complete end-to-end MC based system for gut theranostics after coupling with suitable engineered probiotic senders.

papers.title: Countering Anion Inhibition of Laccase Electron Transfer: Electrostatic Design, Charge-Transfer Dynamics on a Superconducting Quantum Processor, and Its Limits
papers.abstract: Hydroxide at neutral-to-alkaline pH and halides inhibit fungal laccases and limit their use in wastewater treatment. From GFN2-xTB cluster models of Trametes versicolor laccase (PDB 1GYC) we build a four-site Hubbard model of the His454-T3A-T3B-His452 junction of the trinuclear copper cluster and execute its charge-transfer dynamics on the Euro-Q-Exa quantum computer (IQM, 8 qubits, Trotterized circuits with Pauli twirling; 726 jobs). The charge-transfer frequency is measured to 3-5 meV, reproducibly over nine days and across changes of the device qubit map: hydroxide raises the charge-transfer energy of the crystal-geometry model by 92.0 +/- 2.2 meV (exact 87) and exceeds fluoride by 10.1 +/- 1.8 meV. A screen of charged probes in three dielectric models identifies Y116E; in the probe model the hardware resolves a reduction of the hydroxide penalty by 74 +/- 7 meV and of the halide penalty by 64 +/- 5 meV, acting on the site-energy gap rather than on the coupling. A real Glu116 (five conformers) with PROPKA protonation states and the coupled Asp456 gives a realistic reduction of 10-30 meV, with the same sign in 28 of 28 model combinations; the direction and ordering are the prediction, rate factors only an illustration. Scanning the on-site repulsion reverses the sign of the hydroxide effect, and a one-electron Hartree model reproduces the reversal: the measured dynamics is effectively single-particle. On a Fermi-Hubbard benchmark the hardware does not resolve electron correlation; it would need a contrast loss below 0.13 percent per CZ gate instead of the measured 0.34-0.54 percent.

papers.title: 3D-VASE: Volumetric-Aware Scalable and Efficient Multi-Layer Design Synthesis for 3D-Printed Microfluidics
papers.abstract: Additive manufacturing (3D printing) enables complex multi-layer microfluidic devices, but the physical synthesis of passive-flow designs remains a key bottleneck. In such systems, designers must encode timing synchronization and target dosing directly into channel geometry, even though the available routing space across multiple 3D layers is often highly congested, which makes scaling to complex designs difficult. Existing approaches formulate placement, routing, and fluidic constraints as a single monolithic optimization, leading to combinatorial explosion and poor performance on complex designs. This paper presents a volumetric-aware two-stage synthesis framework that decouples global structure from routing detail. A Mixed-Integer Programming (MIP) model first computes a compact multi-layer placement, followed by a dynamic 3D routing engine that enforces timing and volumetric constraints during path construction. To further improve routability in dense layouts, we introduce a hierarchical conflict resolution strategy combining local rip-up-and-reroute with controlled global expansion. Experimental results show that, under timing and volumetric constraints, 3D-VASE consistently improves synthesis speed and, in most test cases, also improves layout quality. Notably, for difficult large-scale cases where prior methods often failed to return any solution within the time limit, 3D-VASE produces feasible high-quality layouts within practical runtimes. These advances enable fast, iterative design-space exploration for complex 3D-printed microfluidic systems.

papers.title: Noise Characterization and Robust Signal Detection in Yeast Pheromone Molecular Communication
papers.abstract: A critical aspect of Molecular Communications (MC) is the implementation of signal detection policies amidst noise. To date, noise characterizations within the MC field have predominantly drawn from methodologies found in wireless communications literature. In this study, we diverge from existing MC research by utilizing a newly developed experimental platform that employs yeast, allowing us to consider more realistic noise characterizations based on the relevant signaling pathways. We propose suitable signal detection mechanisms tailored to this experimental setup, which focuses on yeast cell-to-cell communications. Our analysis identifies gene transcription as the primary source of noise, and we utilize a Markov birth-death process model with Poisson arrivals and departures to characterize it. The noisy expression of the FUS1 gene is best represented using a mixed Gaussian distribution model. This model serves as a foundation for evaluating the performance of Maximum Likelihood Detection mechanisms in terms of Bit Error Rate (BER) for both symbol-by-symbol and sequence transmission schemes. Error analysis indicates that appropriate adjustments to the signal threshold can reduce errors to as low as 10%, which is not negligible. In contrast, the detection of symbol sequences demonstrates enhanced error performance, achieving error rates as low as 0.4%, albeit at the cost of increased computational complexity.

papers.title: Supervised Learning Approaches for Static and Temporal Force Prediction in a Biohybrid Muscle Ring Actuator
papers.abstract: Skeletal muscle-based biohybrid actuators have proved to be a promising component in soft robotics, offering efficient movement. However, their intrinsic biological variability and nonlinearity pose significant challenges for controllability and predictability. To address these issues, this study investigates the application of supervised learning, a form of machine learning, to model and predict the behavior of biohybrid machines (BHMs), focusing on a muscle ring anchored on flexible polymer pillars. First, static prediction models (i.e., random forest and neural network regressors) are trained to estimate the maximum exerted force achieved from input variables such as muscle sample, electrical stimulation parameters, and baseline exerted force. Second, a dynamic modeling framework, based on Long Short-Term Memory networks, is developed to replicate the time series of exerted forces observed. Both modeling approaches demonstrate high predictive accuracy. The best performance of the static models is characterized by a mean R2 of 0.9346, whereas the dynamic model achieves a mean R2 of 0.9944 over five training instances. The static models can enable optimization of muscle actuator performance for targeted applications and required force outcomes, while the dynamic model provides a foundation for developing robustly adaptive control strategies in future biohybrid robotic systems.

papers.title: Human-Data Interaction, Exploration, and Visualization Systems in the AI Era: Challenges and Opportunities
papers.abstract: The rapid advancement of AI is transforming human-centered systems, with profound implications for human-AI interaction, human-data interaction, and visual analytics. In the AI era, data analysis increasingly involves large-scale, heterogeneous, and multimodal data that is predominantly unstructured, as well as foundation models such as LLMs and VLMs, which introduce additional uncertainty into analytical processes. These shifts expose persistent challenges for human-data interactive systems, including perceptually misaligned latency, scalability constraints, limitations of existing interaction and exploration paradigms, and growing uncertainty regarding the reliability and interpretability of AI-generated insights. Responding to these challenges requires moving beyond conventional efficiency and scalability metrics, redefining the roles of humans and machines in analytical workflows, and incorporating cognitive, perceptual, and design principles into every level of the human-data interaction stack. This paper investigates the challenges introduced by recent advances in AI and examines how these developments are reshaping the ways users engage with data, while outlining limitations and open research directions for building human-centered AI systems for interactive data analysis in the AI era.

papers.title: QuantumXCT: Learning Interaction-Induced State Transformation in Cell-Cell Communication via Quantum Entanglement and Generative Modeling
papers.abstract: Inferring cell-cell communication (CCC) from single-cell transcriptomic data remains challenging. Most existing methods retrieve curated ligand-receptor pairs, score their coordinated average expression and apply statistical testing, a static and indirect strategy that tends to overlook intracellular signaling consequences, context dependence and higher-order interactions. Here, we introduce QuantumXCT, a hybrid quantum-classical framework that defines CCC as learnable transformations between cellular state distributions induced by cell-cell interaction. By encoding transcriptomic profiles into a high-dimensional Hilbert space, QuantumXCT trains parameterized quantum circuits to learn a unitary transformation mapping a baseline non-interacting cellular state to an interacting state, and infers CCC under explicitly stated modeling assumptions. Unlike methods restricted to curated ligand-receptor pairs, QuantumXCT can evaluate any cross-cell gene pair. On synthetic data with known ground-truth interactions, QuantumXCT ranked the programmed intercellular interactions above non-interacting gene pairs (ROC-AUC 0.93). On an ovarian cancer-fibroblast mono- and co-culture model, it identified a PDGFB-PDGFRB-STAT3 axis reproducible across bootstrap resamples, amplitude encodings and search algorithms, and consistent with published perturbation experiments. The learned circuit is interpretable: its entangling topology translates into interaction networks, and post hoc contribution analysis quantifies the influence of individual interactions on the observed state transitions. QuantumXCT provides an interpretable, hypothesis-generating framework for de novo discovery of communication programs, and delineates both the potential and the current limits of quantum machine learning in single-cell biology.
